title: Insert Into a Sorted Calendar
statement:
A calendar is a list of busy blocks, blocks[i] = [start, end], covering every time from start to end inclusive. The list is sorted by start, and the blocks are separated: each block ends strictly before the next one starts.

Add the block extra and return the new calendar in the same form: sorted, with no two blocks overlapping or touching. Blocks that overlap extra, or touch it (share an end point, like [1, 4] and [4, 6]), merge with it into one block.

examples.why: [7, 11] overlaps two blocks. The merged block starts at 6 and ends at 14, the end of the last block it swallowed, not at 11.
The new block fits in the gap and merges with nothing. It still has to go in the right place.
The blocks touch at 5, so they merge.

hints: The input is already sorted and separated, so you do not need to sort. Think of the blocks as falling into three groups relative to extra.
Blocks that end before extra starts are untouched and come first. Blocks that start after extra ends are untouched and come last. Everything in between merges.
Walk once: copy blocks with end < extra.start; then, while start ≤ extra.end, widen extra to the min start and max end; push it; copy the rest.

explain.intuition:
Because the calendar is sorted and its blocks are separated, every block falls into one of three runs relative to the new block. First come the blocks that end before extra starts: they cannot touch it and stay as they are. Last come the blocks that start after extra ends: also untouched. Everything in between overlaps or touches extra, and since the blocks are sorted, that middle part is one contiguous run.

So a single pass does it: copy the first run, fold the middle run into extra by taking the smallest start and the largest end, output the merged block, copy the last run. It is like adding a booking to a sorted list of reserved slots in a date picker: you never need to re-sort, only to find where the new slot lands and what it swallows.
steps: Copy every block with end < extra[0] into the result.
While the next block has start ≤ extra[1], it overlaps or touches: set extra[0] = min(extra[0], start) and extra[1] = max(extra[1], end).
pitfalls: Ending the merged block at extra's own end. In example 1 the swallowed block [10, 14] reaches past 11.
Using < instead of ≤ in the overlap test, which leaves touching blocks such as [3, 5] and [5, 9] separate.
Forgetting to output extra when it merges with nothing, or when it belongs after every block.

solutions.title: Append, sort and merge
solutions.idea: Add the new block to the list, sort by start, and run the standard merge. Correct, but it throws away the fact that the input was already sorted.

solutions.title: One pass in three runs
solutions.idea: Copy the blocks before, fold the overlapping run into the new block, copy the blocks after.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def insertBlock(self, blocks: List[List[int]], extra: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        out = []
        s, e = extra
        i, n = 0, len(blocks)
        while i < n and blocks[i][1] < s:
            out.append(blocks[i])
            i += 1
        while i < n and blocks[i][0] <= e:
            s = min(s, blocks[i][0])
            e = max(e, blocks[i][1])
            i += 1
        out.append([s, e])
        out.extend(blocks[i:])
        return out

followups: The output still costs O(n) to build. If the calendar were stored so that you could find the first and last affected block by binary search, what would the search part cost?
Insert many new blocks one after another. When is it better to collect them and merge once?
